A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with complete, readable main text and Appendices A–K. Corresponding equations, figures, experimental descriptions, and references support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v4 reports original synthetic ridge-regression experiments measuring risks and variance components, including correlated forecasting tests. Figures 1–4, 6, and Appendix J compare empirical measurements with theoretical predictions.

after.justification: v5 retains these original experiments, including empirical risk measurements and error bars across repeated datasets in the main text and Appendix J.

M1.justification: The ridge objective, CorrGCV computation, correlated-test extension, and implementation in Section 4 and Appendix A are unchanged. The risk-label correction does not alter the computational procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic regression coverage: isotropic and structured covariates, exponential, nearest-neighbor and power-law correlations, mismatched noise correlations, and correlated forecasting tests.

E2.justification: The comparisons retain ordinary GCV (Naive GCV1), Altman's correction (Naive GCV2), and Carmack et al.'s GCCV in Figure 10. No comparator is added or removed from a corresponding experiment.

E3.justification: The reported dimensions, sample-size and ridge sweeps, noise settings, and forecasting procedures are unchanged. Figure 6 already evaluated out-of-sample risk in v4, so the theorem's corrected terminology does not establish an evaluation-metric change.

E4.justification: The scaling, double-descent, noise-mismatch, and prediction-horizon analyses are retained. Appendices E–J contain the same spectral checks, resolution and degrees-of-freedom analyses, and empirical duality checks.

E5.justification: Appendix K identically states that error bars use ten regression runs over different datasets. The figure captions retain the same uncertainty-reporting practice; no run-count, seed, or statistical-procedure changes appear.

E6.justification: The corresponding plots retain their numerical results, curves, empirical markers, and error bars throughout the main text and appendices. No result entries or empirical findings are added, removed, or revised.

T1.justification: Theorem 5.1 and Appendix C.5 replace R_g with R_out in the multiplicative correlated-test risk relation. Section 1 defines R_g as excess risk, whereas the proof includes test-label noise. This corrects the theorem's stated quantity; the correlation factor, assumptions, and derivation remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: sharp correlated-sample risk asymptotics, asymptotically exact CorrGCV under matched correlations, and extensions to correlated test points.

C2.justification: The interpretations of forecasting optimism, correlation effects on double descent, and noise mismatch are retained. The limitations concerning matrix-Gaussian assumptions, unproved universality for dependent data, and dimension-free bounds are also unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix A retains the same JAX code and S-transform estimation instructions. Appendix K retains the hardware and compute disclosures, and the code-access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning are unchanged, including the discussion of previous GCV corrections and the complementary relationship to Luo et al. (2024).

P1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C.5 receive localized risk-terminology and notation corrections, and the arXiv version/date stamp is updated. The narrative, section order, and appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: The corrected risk labels produce slight equation-spacing and line-wrap adjustments on pages 8–9 and 24. Figures 1–19 retain their panels, axes, legends, captions, and placement; there is no figure or table redesign.

improvement.justification: v5 resolves the inconsistency between Theorem 5.1's excess-risk notation and the total-risk calculation already present in Appendix C.5. Identifying the affected quantity as R_out helps prevent applying the multiplicative correction to the wrong risk definition. This is a limited improvement in mathematical precision, with the method and empirical support preserved.
